title: Education Suddenly Changed, and I Didn't See It Coming
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that the most important shift in English education is happening on YouTube, where Katharine Birbalsingh of Michaela Community School launched a professionally produced channel three months ago. He points to her numbers (49,000 subscribers after eight videos, a 538,000-view hit) as evidence that parents, not just teachers, are hungry for a school that prioritises good behaviour. He notes that critics of Michaela's discipline can only attack it philosophically, because there are no exposes of shouting teachers or unhappy staff, and that its results outperform every other secondary school. Salles reads Birbalsingh's spread-the-word strategy as a better bet than the empire-building of multi-academy trusts, since ideas travel on shocks and cracks such as funding squeezes, SEND pressure and head teacher exits. He adds that lifestyle YouTuber Unjaded Jade is also gaining views on education content, which suggests wide disaffection with the schooling people received. He closes by urging anyone who cares about education, and not only teaching, to start a channel.
points: Birbalsingh's YouTube channel shows that a behaviour-first model of schooling has a large public audience far beyond teachers, since most of her views came from people the algorithm took months to find.
Salles contends that Michaela's critics rely on philosophical objections because they cannot point to abuse, staff complaints or weak results.
His account of how ideas spread contrasts the slow trust-and-franchise model of academy chains with viral, direct-to-parent messaging that rides on funding and SEND pressure.
The success of an unrelated wellness YouTuber's education videos is offered as evidence that even young adults are deeply dissatisfied with the schooling they received.
The practical advice is that educators who care about policy, not only classroom craft, should build a public presence on video now.
quotes: Since 2017 I’ve been protesting at the viral ability of social media to spread stupid ideas. It has savaged English teaching, where the two default teaching methods are now annotation and teaching paragraph structures.
After only 8 videos she has over 49,000 subscribers. That’s an outlier among outliers. In three months she has had nearly 800,000 views.

There are plenty of attacks against the cult-like approach to discipline at Michaela. But they are all philosphical. There are no exposes of teachers shouting and screaming at kids, because there is no shouting and screaming at kids.
Few of the attackers deal with the uncomfortable fact that every year Michaela’s students outperform every other secondary school in the country.
New ideas do not spread on even ground. They spread when their are cracks, earthquakes, sudden shifts as the ground is thrust upwards for winners and sucked downwards for the losers.
Even twenty somethings are hugely disaffected by the education they have received. It is astonishing that this pivot in content has led to increased, rather than decreased views.

If you care passionately about education (rather than only teaching), now is the time to start a YouTube channel. The public cares, and that means politicians will care, and that means the revolution is coming.
